extracted.intended_audience: students, teachers, and practitioners of literary criticism; readers learning to evaluate poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for close reading and practical criticism of poems, focusing on how readers understand meaning, avoid common errors, and improve discriminating response. Emphasises psychological, social, and pedagogical factors that affect critical judgement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of author reputation (avoid idolising)
rubrics_metrics.description: When we know we are reading Milton or Shelley much of our approval is accorded to an idol; conversely knowledge of a lesser author can bring patronising condescension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attempt to read without guidance of reputation (anonymous reading) to discover how much tradition and reputation bias response; be aware that knowing the author trains our response like a wire for a climbing plant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading without traditional guidance (anonymous reading)
rubrics_metrics.description: The attempt to read without tradition's guidance is a strain but salutary; it reveals our dependence on tradition and the dangers thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice anonymous reading to learn how inattentive ordinary reading of established poetry often is, but recognise limits and potential difficulties of this method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgement of variability in individual critical capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual readers vary widely in quality of discernment, passing from high discernment to startling obtuseness even with contiguous poems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect and allow for variability; do not generalise from single episodes. Be cautious about fatigue and situational effects; consider limiting number of poems per session (author suggests four poems may be too many for a week's reading).

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for situational and physical influences on reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Health, wakefulness, distractions, hunger, air quality, humidity, light, and pervasive noises (e.g., modern transport) all affect our capacity to respond to verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating responses, control for environmental and bodily conditions; recognise that many failures of response arise from these irrelevant influences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish social/phatic responses from poem-derived criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: In public and hurried conditions, much critical chitchat is social gesture ('phatic communion') rather than commentary arising from the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not mistake polite or spleen-driven remarks for genuine criticism; be alert to 'imitation currency'—stock replies critics use in emergencies—and insist on evidence that the poem itself prompted the response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation between sensitivity to poetry and general imaginative life
rubrics_metrics.description: Insensitiveness to poetry often reflects a low level of general imaginative life; poetry is a secret discipline requiring initiation and technique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat poetry-reading as a cultivated skill that can be taught; consider poetry as a means to strengthen minds' capacity to order themselves and to make poetic language more accessible to the educated individual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution about misuse of psychology in criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistical inquiries, crude psychoanalytic or behaviourist approaches, and attempts to explain masterpieces from a first encounter are liable to make readers uncomfortable and to do harm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reject simplistic or dogmatic psychological metrics (counts of imagery, measurements of 'emotional response', etc.); welcome cautious, well-informed psychological inquiry that respects poetic complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against squeamishness about psychological dissection
rubrics_metrics.description: The prejudice that close psychological analysis will 'murder' poetry is misplaced; dissection harms only pathological minds or those with weak interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permit careful psychological analysis that observes fine distinctions and preserves values; hasten development of a naturalistic psychology that records facts without demolishing necessary literary values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'prudential use' of language (formulaic fluency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many people use words because they know how they are ordinarily used rather than because they have precise ideas—this is termed a 'prudential' use of language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics and readers should seek understanding beyond apt manoeuvring of words or rehearsed locutions; test whether paraphrase or description indicates genuine discrimination rather than learned formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish levels/senses of 'understanding'
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding ranges from mere perception of words' sound/shape, to prompt action or emotion, to intellectual discrimination (distinguishing 'This' from 'That'), and higher forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing comprehension, identify which level is in operation; do not conflate recognition of words with deeper intellectual or emotional understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate the four functions of language: sense (thought), feeling, tone, intention
rubrics_metrics.description: Language simultaneously conveys thought (sense), excites feeling, signals tone (attitude toward listener), and implies intention (desire, active direction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good understanding requires receiving each contributory meaning separately where possible; training should aim to disentangle these functions in passages under scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid confusing one language function for another
rubrics_metrics.description: A common error is to mistake feeling for statement, to take expression of tone for intention, or to read a modification due to tone as irrelevant intention—confusions increase with figurative language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully disentangle metaphorical and figurative usages; use paraphrase and attentive analysis to detect misinterpretations (Richards' experiments found many university readers misinterpret such language).

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware 'dictionary understanding' as an insidious substitute
rubrics_metrics.description: Replacing precise thought or feeling by a cluster of synonymous words ('I mean comprehending, grasping the sense...') conceals limitations of real understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Test depth of comprehension beyond verbal substitutions; require demonstration (description, action, or nuanced paraphrase) rather than acceptance of synonymous locutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discern order and proportion among contributory meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: Perfect understanding involves accurate direction of thought, correct evocation of feeling, exact apprehension of tone, and precise recognition of intention, all in their right order and proportion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether feeling, thought, tone, and intention stand in proper relations; watch for maladaptive dominance (e.g., feeling governing thought) which can ruin a passage even if components are individually sound.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise direct vs reflective apprehension of feeling/tone/intention
rubrics_metrics.description: One can either undergo the feeling/tone/intention directly (adopt it) or think of it (perceive/describe it), and mistakes are possible in both modes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging understanding, note whether a reader actually undergos the feeling or merely reports it; both forms are valid but distinct and subject to different errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of analytic practice for improving discernment
rubrics_metrics.description: Discernment of the order among contributory meanings may be aided by practice in analysis—analysis is necessary for judgement though not identical with the formed receptive whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use careful analytic exercises (paraphrase, separation of functions, order-testing) in teaching to improve the capacity to discern total meaning in reading.
